After the first two days of the Global Off-Grid Solar Forum and Expo ( #GOGSFE24 ) in Nairobi, Kenya, some clear key messages are being shared with one voice across all stakeholders, including policymakers, industry leaders, business associations, development partners, and civil society organizations (CSOs):

1. Off-grid renewable energy solutions are the most cost-effective way to bridge the energy access gap while driving significant sustainable development benefits.
2. The business and financial models to address high financing costs already exist—there’s no need to reinvent the wheel.
3. Enforceable policy and regulatory frameworks are critical for unlocking private capital and scaling off-grid renewable energy solutions.
4. It is essential to integrate off-grid renewable energy solutions into broader energy sector planning.
5. Addressing the local currency financing challenges is fundamental to expanding off-grid renewable energy solutions.

A recurring theme through all these points is the need for deliberate partnerships among key stakeholders—no single partner can do it all. This is why I’m excited about how the African Minigrid Programme's building blocks will feed into the bold M300 initiative by the World Bank, the African Development Bank, and other partners.

We have the blueprint to address the energy access gap, and now is the time to implement it. Let’s roll up our sleeves and move forward boldly, together, to bring real change to the ground. Africa Minigrids Program

Today, I am raising the alarm.
 
Together with the Troika of COP28 UAE, COP29 Azerbaijan, COP30 Brazil Presidencies and the Global Renewables Alliance (GRA), IRENA published a report that tracks progress towards tripling renewables and doubling energy efficiency by 2030.

And as the custodian agency tasked with tracking and reporting on progress towards 2030, IRENA concludes that progress falls short. 

The landmark #UAEConsensus agreed at COP28 is critical for our global efforts to keep 1.5°C within reach but we are at risk of missing our collective goal.

Some key facts:

1- Despite an unprecedented growth in renewable power additions of 473 GW in 2023, it is far from enough. The world must add on average 1044 GW every year. 

2- Current Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) will only add 1.5 TW of renewable power capacity by 2030, but we need more than 7 TW.
 
3- Global investments in renewables reached a record of USD 570 billion in 2023 but it must triple to USD 1.5 trillion annually. 

Furthermore, current investment patterns are disproportionately concentrated in advanced economies and a few large emerging markets like China, India, and Brazil. The rest of the developing world remains underserved, receiving just 10% of global energy investments. This imbalance threatens not only the pace of energy transition but also the equitable distribution of its benefits.
 
It is still possible to achieve our goals, but it requires immediate global action to overcome the structural and systemic barriers that impede progress. Significant progress is needed across key enablers of the energy transition, namely: infrastructure and system operation, policy, supply chains and skills, finance and international collaboration. 

The next round of NDCs in 2025 must close the gaps. And an agreement on a robust New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) of climate finance at COP29 will be vital for enhancing financial support for climate action in the Global South.

Read ‘Delivering on the UAE Consensus: Tracking progress toward tripling renewable energy capacity and doubling energy efficiency by 2030’ that was released today at the PreCOP to inform national delegations and negotiators in the run up to COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan. 👇

✅ Esther Muringo Wang’ombe, Director Renewable Energy at the Ministry of Energy of Kenya
✅ Laura Muñoz Pérez, United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF) Regional Manager for West Africa
✅ Avinash Persaud, Special Advisor on Climate Change to the President of the Inter-American Development Bank
✅ Oscar Njuguna, Group Director, Sustainability at Equity Bank Limited.

The speakers emphasised how partnerships are vital in developing, de-risking, and financing #CleanEnergy projects across Africa. Through #EnergyForGrowth in Africa, UNDP aims to leverage its on-the-ground expertise and coordinate infrastructure initiatives to transform Africa's clean energy sector, fostering growth and sustainability.

Thank you to our partners, speakers, and panellists who contributed to an inspiring discussion on how concessional finance and technical assistance can unlock capital, build strong investment environments, and advance Africa’s clean energy agenda.

1. Support countries in creating bankable energy projects integrated with their NDCs, ensuring these plans are actionable and backed by comprehensive sectoral investment analyses.
2. ⁠Promote financial innovation & implement tools like credit guarantees and blended finance, facilitating debt-smart energy transition financing in developing countries.
3. ⁠Leverage digital technologies to help identify optimal investment opportunities, ensure optimized off-grid solutions & enable data-driven policymaking.

UNDP  and United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  are supporting these efforts by scaling up capital for renewable energy and developing innovative guarantee schemes that provide safety nets for investors and lenders, reducing perceived risks to move renewable energy projects from pipeline to financial closure.

🏛️Policymakers are pivotal to create #regulatory frameworks, to create #offtake through #mandates and to initiate supply by economic support.
🌐International organizations should establish global #rules and support adoption through robust #certification.
⛽Fuel suppliers will need to secure sustainable energy feedstocks through upstream investments and #partnerships.
🏗 Manufacturers should develop engines/vessels for synthetic fuels and invest in R&D to unlock #efficiency gains.
🛂 Airports/port authorities will need to set up refueling infrastructure and ensure constant low-carbon fuel supply.
✈️🚢Airlines/shipping companies can play a central role by commercialization of sustainable options and development of #multistakeholder and #multilevel partnerships.

Clean cooking signifies more than just technological change; it is a powerful catalyst for a domino effect of outcomes – improved health, environmental protection, and economic empowerment. Yet, 2.1 billion people still depend on polluting and harmful fuels for this basic need. 

Recognizing this urgent challenge, G20 leaders at G20 Brasil 2024 this week reaffirmed their commitment to accelerate efforts to achieve universal clean cooking access by 2030. ☀️

With over 90% of people without clean cooking access also lacking the funding and policy environments for effective interventions, the ‘Roadmap for the Brazil G20 Presidency’s Clean Cooking Strategy’’—to which UNDP is honored to have contributed feedback—addresses these gaps by outlining actionable guidance to establish enabling policies and achieve universal clean cooking access by 2030 through four key pillars:

1. Enhancing policy and regulatory frameworks
2. Identifying and scaling innovative financing models
3. Strengthening markets and developing robust clean cooking supply chains
4. Assessing impact, sharing knowledge, and collecting data to support decision-making

Achieving universal clean cooking is within reach but demands strong political will. Success hinges on integrating clean cooking into climate pledges and national electrification strategies while mobilizing the $8 billion annually needed through data-driven policies, innovative financing, and collaboration between governments, NGOs, the private sector, and the communities we aim to empower. 💡
